title: Training vs Facilitation: How to Tell Which One Your Session Needs
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that sessions fail when a leader runs training for a group that needed to decide something together, or runs facilitation for a group that lacked the knowledge to contribute. He sets out five differences: who does the talking, where the content comes from, what success looks like, how the room is arranged, and what happens afterward. In training the trainer holds the content and talks most of the time, while in facilitation the group supplies the content and the facilitator runs the process. Training succeeds when people can do something new, whereas facilitation succeeds when the group produces a decision or plan. He notes that facilitated outputs fade quickly unless each commitment has an owner and a check-in date within 14 days. Most real sessions need both, so he advises asking, block by block, whether participants need to learn something or build something, and announcing the switch to the room.
points: Record your next session and compare your talking time to the group's work time; above about 30% you are closer to training than facilitation.
Training content comes from the expert, so novices asked to facilitate their own answers will only guess, while experienced groups can build on what they know.
Judge each format by its own measure: learning for training, and decisions or commitments for facilitation.
Group decisions decay fast, so every commitment needs a named owner and a check-in booked within 14 days before people leave.
For mixed sessions, design each agenda block as learn or build, change the room at the switch and tell participants which mode they are in.
quotes: In training, the trainer talks most of the time. Somewhere around 70-80%. They hold the content and the group receives it.
Above about 30%, you’re closer to training than facilitation, whatever the invite called it.
Training succeeds when people learn the thing. Can they do something this afternoon that they couldn’t do this morning?
A facilitated session judged on “what did you learn?” scores badly on the feedback form, even when the team walked out with the plan they came for.
Facilitation fades fast. The output is a set of group decisions, and a group decision only holds while the group keeps it up.
Every commitment that leaves the room needs an owner and a check-in date within 14 days.
Most “can you train our team on communication?” requests turn out to mean “can you help our team agree how they’ll communicate?
